newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany says it will meet EMU deficit goal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany says it will meet EMU deficit goal.

text.p: The German government on Friday rejected mounting speculation that it would miss borrowing targets this year, saying it would meet the deficit goal set in the Maastricht Treaty to qualify for European monetary union.

A government spokeswoman dismissed newspaper reports that climbing unemployment would force Finance Minister Theo Waigel to miss his budget deficit objective of below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"Germany will be below the three percent deficit criterion," Finance Ministry spokeswoman Barbara Eckrich said in answer to a question at a news conference.

Germany has staked a lot of political capital on hitting the deficit goal, urging strict compliance by other would-be members to ensure the euro is as strong as the mark and is not watered down by the addition of weaker currencies.
Eckrich was responding to a report in the Handelsblatt daily which said concerns were mounting within the government that Germany's deficit would overshoot.

Handelsblatt and other newspapers have said in reports sourced to unnamed officials that Waigel would freeze spending this month to try to meet his federal deficit target of 53.3 billion marks ($33.2 billion).
But Eckrich said no decision had been taken on a spending crackdown before a review by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet of the government's annual economic report on January 28.
Ministers directly involved in economic policy will review the report's findings on January 24.
Handelsblatt said Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt now expected that unemployment, which hit a seasonally-adjusted post-war record of 4.1 million in December, would average 4.2 million this year.

That is over 200,000 above the prediction last autumn by independent economists and institutes, on whose forecasts the budget is based. Extra jobless benefits of six billion marks and tax revenue losses of two billion could result, it said.

High unemployment drove down tax receipts last year and caused a blowout in the social security budget which led Waigel to overshoot his budgeted federal deficit of 59.9 billion marks by 18.4 billion marks.
As a result, the total public sector deficit -- comprising Bonn, regional states and municipalities -- rose to 3.9 percent of GDP last year from 3.5 percent the year before.
Eckrich said, however, that Waigel's goal of meeting and beating the Maastricht deficit ceiling this year still left room for tax revenues to fall short of official projections.
She declined to comment on whether Germany's economy would meet official growth forecasts of 2.5 percent this year, also made last autumn.
Handelsblatt said Rexrodt was sticking to the forecast and he expected German GDP to expand by 2.0-2.5 percent in 1998.
Bank economists say the fiscal tightening envisaged in this year's budget -- when federal spending will fall in real terms by some two percent -- could put a drag on economic recovery.
And, Handelsblatt said, the deflationary environment could also hit nominal growth and lead to lower tax receipts.
